title: Occasion: Catherine Wordsworth (1808-1812)
short: An elegy for Wordsworth's daughter Catherine, who died on 4 June 1812, aged three; published in Poems (1815).
body: Wordsworth told Isabella Fenwick that the sonnet 'was in fact suggested by my daughter Catherine long after her death'. Catherine was born on 6 September 1808 and died on 4 June 1812; her brother Thomas died later the same year. Wordsworth placed the poem among his 'Miscellaneous Sonnets' in 1815. The sonnet records a moment, months or years later, when the poet felt a sudden happiness and turned to share it with her before remembering she was dead. C. S. Lewis took the opening phrase as the title of his autobiography Surprised by Joy (1955).

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 6 (1896), headnote, Fenwick note and variants
Juliet Barker, Wordsworth: A Life (London: Viking, 2000)

title: impatient as the Wind
short: The impulse to share joy is as sudden and uncontrollable as wind; the capital W personifies it.
body: The simile captures the instinctive speed of the turn: before thought intervenes, he has already turned. The dash after 'Wind' and the run-on into line 2 enact the movement. Wind in Wordsworth is often a figure for spontaneous feeling (compare the 'correspondent breeze' of The Prelude, Book I). Here the impulse that feels like freedom becomes the occasion of fresh grief.

title: I turned (1815: 'I wished')
short: The 1815 text read 'I wished to share the transport'; from 1820 'I turned', a physical action rather than a mere desire.
body: Knight records that 1815 read 'I wished' and that 'I turned' appears from 1820. The revision makes the moment bodily and instinctive: he actually turns, as if she were in the room, which makes the recognition more painful. The change is a good example of Wordsworth's lifelong revision of his poems. 'Turned' also anticipates 'That thought's return' in line 9: the poem is built on turnings of body and mind, from the impulse to share joy to the return of grief.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 6 (1896), headnote, Fenwick note and variants

title: transport
short: Rapture, ecstatic joy; the sense of being carried out of oneself.
body: 'Transport' meant a state of being 'carried away' by strong emotion, especially delight (OED, from Latin transportare, to carry across). It echoes 'joy' in line 1 and sets up the shock of 'Oh! with whom / But Thee': there is no one else he would share it with. The word belongs to the elevated eighteenth-century vocabulary for strong feeling, and its conventionality makes the collapse into 'Oh! with whom' all the more abrupt.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, 'transport'

title: deep buried in the silent tomb
short: 1815 read 'long buried'; the later 'deep buried' stresses distance and finality rather than time.
body: Knight records the 1815 reading 'long buried', changed to 'deep buried' in 1820. 'Long' fitted the Fenwick note's 'long after her death'; 'deep' stresses how far beyond reach she is. Catherine was buried in Grasmere churchyard. Note the double space in this text after 'buried', a typesetting accident. The silent tomb contrasts with the impulse to speak and share: the one person he turns to is the one who can no longer hear.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 6 (1896), headnote, Fenwick note and variants
Juliet Barker, Wordsworth: A Life (London: Viking, 2000)

title: vicissitude
short: Change, the alternation of fortune; the tomb is the one place change cannot reach.
body: From Latin vicissitudo, change or alternation (OED). The line is grimly double: the grave is beyond the changes of fortune that bring joy and sorrow to the living, but it is also beyond the reach of the very change of feeling that the poem has just experienced. The question mark makes the whole of lines 1-4 a cry: with whom else would I share joy?

title: Love, faithful love
short: It was love that made him think of her, and yet the same love seems to have betrayed her by forgetting.
body: The repetition 'Love, faithful love' asserts constancy at the very moment the speaker accuses himself of forgetting. The paradox drives the octave: love recalled her to mind, so how could he have forgotten her, even for an instant? The self-reproach is the subject of the poem as much as the grief. 'Recalled thee to my mind' is literal, since love's impulse brought her to mind, and ironic, since that same impulse shows she had for a moment been absent from it.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 6 (1896), headnote, Fenwick note and variants

anchor: the least division of an hour
title: the least division of an hour
short: Even the smallest fraction of time; the forgetting lasted only a moment, yet feels unforgivable.
body: 'Division' is the term for a fraction or subdivision of time (OED). The careful, almost legalistic phrase measures how short the lapse was and how seriously he takes it. Elegies traditionally lament that the dead are forgotten by the world; here the elegist convicts himself. The phrase suggests the hour divided into minutes, making the lapse measurable and so, to the speaker's conscience, inexcusable.

title: beguiled
short: Deceived, diverted; tricked into forgetting by the passing pleasure.
body: 'Beguile' means to deceive or charm away (OED); it can also mean to while away time pleasantly, a sense that adds bitterness here. Being 'blind / To my most grievous loss' completes the image: joy made him blind, and the return of sight brings the 'worst pang'. The line break after 'blind' throws weight onto 'To my most grievous loss', and the question mark closes the long sentence that began at 'Through what power'.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, 'beguile'

title: Petrarchan sonnet and mid-line turn
short: A Petrarchan sonnet (abbaacca dedede) whose turn falls in the middle of line 9, after the octave's question.
body: The octave rhymes Wind/find/mind/blind and whom/tomb/power/hour; the sestet alternates return/forlorn/unborn with bore/more/restore. Instead of a break between octave and sestet, the question runs on into line 9, and the turn ('That thought's return') comes mid-line, enacting the jolt of remembering. Wordsworth had revived the Miltonic sonnet in 1802, and Milton's practice of carrying sense across the octave is visible here.

sources.cite: William Knight, ed., The Poetical Works of William Wordsworth, vol. 6 (1896), headnote, Fenwick note and variants

title: the worst pang, save one
short: The second grief equals all but the first: the moment he first knew she was dead.
body: The phrase 'Save one, one only' insists on exactness, as if grading pains. The original grief was learning that his 'heart's best treasure was no more'; Catherine died suddenly, aged three. The present pang, renewing that knowledge, is next worst. 'Forlorn' means abandoned, desolate (OED). The grammar insists on ranking griefs, a precision whose restraint many readers find more moving than open lament.

sources.cite: Juliet Barker, Wordsworth: A Life (London: Viking, 2000)

Oxford English Dictionary, 'forlorn'

title: my heart's best treasure
short: Recalls Jesus' words 'where your treasure is, there will your heart be also' (Matthew 6:21).
body: The sermon contrasts treasure on earth, which moth and rust corrupt, with treasure in heaven. Wordsworth's phrase fits both: his treasure was on earth and is now lost, but the last line calls her face 'heavenly'. The quiet biblical echo hints at Christian consolation without stating it; the sonnet ends on the fact of loss. 'Best' also implies other treasures, his wife and surviving children, without lessening the singularity of this loss.

sources.cite: Bible, King James Version, Matthew 6:19-21

title: that heavenly face
short: No present or future time can restore her face to his sight; the sonnet ends on irreversible loss.
body: 'Neither present time, nor years unborn' covers all time: the face is gone for ever from sight, if not from memory. 'Heavenly' means beautiful and also now in heaven. The final line's inverted syntax (object before verb) places 'restore' last, the word for what cannot happen. Readers compare the earlier poem on Catherine, 'Characteristics of a Child three Years Old' (1811), which Knight cites.
